Our definition relaxes several traditional constraints, allowing the creation of simpler, more feature-laden applications within the Ozy container. Our analysis compares the costs and benefits of distributed orchestration over traditional models, supporting our claim that Ozy can achieve similar results, if not superior, outcomes compared to existing service-based frameworks. Specifically, we highlight differences in performance, scalability, and security across the two approaches, validating the efficiency and reliability of the Ozy architecture. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study indicates that this is indeed the case. We demonstrate specific learning tasks for which learners with computational limitations need significantly more parameters than those with theoretical information bounds. Moreover, our results suggest that robust learning could necessitate even more constraints. Building upon a recent discovery, we further prove that bounded learners with computational limitations require an exponentially larger number of parameters compared to those with theoretical information bounds. Our study indicates that this may not be the case, and we show a learning task where regular learning doesn't effectively prepare the data for robust learning. We also present a strategy to address the critical question of which data preparations can facilitate efficient robust learning within an identical model architecture. Our technique involves deriving parameter requirements for an infinite number of data preparations through a measure of parameter complexity. We illustrate that a substantial portion of this measure lies in the 'intermediate zone,' where neither typical nor robust learning applies. We have proven that parameter complexity in the 'intermediate zone' is exponentially higher than what's achievable through both standard and robust optimization. Our studies show that while standard training can effectively prepare the data for robust learning within the same model architecture, robust training doesn't effectively prepare the data for standard learning, indicating the possibility of divergent learning objectives. Using network visualizations, our analysis further reveals that this inefficiency might be due to robust training's need to'relearn' the patterns that were already learned during standard training. We have established that robust training's 'forgetfulness' of these patterns could be the primary cause of the massive overparameterization required. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. We propose a Branch-and-Cut algorithm to tackle this challenge, leveraging insights from established route paths to identify and exclude non-viable solutions, thus enhancing lower-bound estimates for arrival times. These insights may prove valuable for developing tailored algorithms to tackle these types of problems. Lastly, we recommend adjusting service times in accordance with a proposed model, thereby allowing users to prefer routes with shorter journey times and reduced pool usage. Furthermore, we determined that data exchange settings are either 'uniquely solvable' or'multiply solvable', depending on whether a single or multiple solutions exist, respectively. Ultimately, we have found that uniquely solvable key-covered settings can be effectively resolved through a structured approach and the application of existing RDF data exchange methods. This unique application allows for direct analysis and optimization within the target dependency schema. Finally, we have determined that specific data exchange settings can be deemed 'basicely key-covered', a condition that ensures the existence of a minimal solution, comprising IRIs with base components only. This unique condition facilitates an in-depth analysis of RDF data exchange, as well as an exploration of the differences between basic and uniquely solvable data exchange settings. These distinctions are exemplified through a series of constructed examples. Finally, we have initiated an investigation into incorporating constraints between tuples, building upon a subset of FDs referred to as cFDs. Lastly, we addressed the impact of the finite resolution on the measurement of the Higgs boson mass, yielding a measurable effect, specifically 70 MeV, which is nearly 20\% of the 125 GeV resolution. The limited availability of linguistic diversity in these tools results in inadequate representations of non-English languages within the associated datasets. In response to this problem, we have created the Indic Listening Dataset, a massive collection of audio transcripts from 8 Indic languages. This comprehensive dataset spans various domains and encompasses diverse genres such as conversations, lectures, and podcasts. This theoretical framework allows us to derive an expression for the determinants in question through the finite-temperature free energy of a corresponding spin chain, calculated using the quantum inverse spectral problem solution. This phenomenon is analogous to a phase shift occurring in the corresponding spin chain's thermodynamic behavior. In contrast, the classic co-administered two-drug combination may actually contribute to the emergence of drug-resistant parasites. Employing only raw, unlabeled audio and text data, as well as a dictionary, our technique enables high-quality speech synthesis without requiring a prelabeled dataset. Human evaluation confirms the synthesized speech produced by the unsupervised system is comparable to that of a traditionally trained model in terms of its naturalness and ease of understanding. Furthermore, listener surveys revealed that the unsupervised speech synthesis method we devised laid the groundwork for several future improvements. Based on these results, we believe that the unsupervised speech synthesis approach we devised is a promising subfield of natural language processing. Although the data requirements for it are relatively low compared to other similar methods, it achieves state-of-the-art performance with adequate data. Consequently, it is anticipated that the recent surge in the collection of large, publicly available speech recognition transcriptions will be particularly beneficial for it. As such, we encourage researchers to capitalize on this opportunity by transforming these transcriptions into raw, unlabeled data suitable for speech synthesis. Moreover, we have made the source code for the unsupervised speech synthesis approach we devised available on GitHub at https://github.com/speechunsup/SpeechSynthesis. Specifically, we are seeking contributions in the form of new methods for speech synthesis, speech-to-text translation, and speech emotion recognition. One potential direction for this is the development of unsupervised speech synthesis methods that prioritize specific characteristics, such as voice similarity or the presence of specific content. Another promising direction is the creation of speech synthesis methods that draw upon data from multiple sources, such as speech recognition or text-to-speech, as opposed to the single-source model employed in our work. Lastly, we would like to encourage an expansion of this area into other domains, such as language translation and software translation. Ultimately, the goal of this research is the development of powerful, general-purpose models for speech processing, and it is our hope that the recent breakthroughs achieved through the acquisition of large, properly annotated speech data will be a significant step in this direction

These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of a previous study that combined data from several previous close approaches but based the calculations on data for electron density and solar proton flux only, where the average energy flux was about 60 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 11 Watts. These observations support the idea that heat from the solar core and other forces that expel plasma outward from the sun could be responsible for pushing away the charged particles that make up the solar wind, even in very dense regions that remain intact near the inner edge. They also confirm, further validating previous research, that the solar wind energy flux that reaches the orbit where Earth's gravity holds sway does not seem to be determined by how close the Parker Solar Probe approaches the solar center during its orbits. Its analysis could be applied not just to wind effects but also to understanding the accretion process in these high mass X-ray binaries, and access to similar data could afford still greater insights into these phenomena. It is for this reason that studying accretion and wind interactions in these X-ray binaries is a vital component in the broader field of astrophysics. focusing on the Azimuthally Symmetric Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), a theoretical framework derived from the established equation by Laplace and Poisson. Our findings indicate that, under certain conditions dependent on the object's spin, the ASTG can generate repulsive gravitational fields in the polar regions of massive objects, thereby shedding new light on the phenomenon of outflows as a manifestation of repulsive gravity. This process is an integral component of star formation and has been the subject of extensive debate among astronomers and cosmologists. This paper specifically examines and weighs the feasibility of generating repulsive gravitational fields in astrophysical contexts. To achieve this, we have developed a general method for identifying the conditions under which the ASTG produces a repulsive force at a specific point. Leveraging this method, we have calculated the location of the ASTG's center of mass and determined the total mass within a sphere of radius r. By applying a modified version of the ASTG that only considers masses within a radius r, we have demonstrated for the first time that various astrophysical objects and systems such as neutron stars, black holes, binary systems, globular clusters, the Milky Way, the universe as a whole, the solar system, and binary neutron star mergers could host repulsive gravitational fields in their polar regions. We have further utilized our modified ASTG to address the challenge of achieving stability in stationary, spherically symmetric structures such as black holes and other potential structures that may form as a result of outflows due to repulsive gravity. We have demonstrated that for massive objects, outflows induced by repulsive gravity can lead to space- and time-local negative pressure where gravity is attractive; hence, such expulsion of matter could be interpreted as an manifestation of repulsive gravity. This method is achieved by incorporating an auxiliary rank-2 tensor $B_{ij}$ into the BCFT, with $B_{ij}$ driven by a equation compatible with $\phi_{ij}$ and defined within a time slice of de Sitter space. Additionally, we define a reflection operator that governs $\phi$ in accordance with its Kretchmair-Rahlf algebra on de Sitter space, with this operator being dissected into elements on two time slices. Subsequently, we illustrate the application of this BCFT construction through a calculation of the contribution to $\phi_{ij}$ resulting from its reflection. Furthermore, we construct a different Poincaré and BCFT-invariant reflection operator for spinor $\psi$ by incorporating an auxiliary spinor $\chi$, with this operator being split into elements on two time slices. Following this, we explore the relationship between the constructed BCFT and ICFT. Consequently, we are able to show that a time slice of de Sitter group $D_{4n}$ can be reinterpreted as a slice of anti de Sitter group $D_{4n+2}$, with this reinterpretation utilizing the BCFT construction. Subsequently, we are able to identify the BCFT as an implementation of chiral de Sitter CFT. Finally, we reflect on the implications of our work for the information paradox problem, with particular attention to the problem as it relates to black holes and cosmological de Sitter spaces. In this context, the problem appears to be connectible to quantum computation via the analysis of time-slice teleportation and the assessment of the maximum information-transferring capacity of a time slice via the use of reflection operators. Subsequently, the black hole's surface can be reinterpreted as an ICFT and BCFT-reflecting anti de Sitter surface. With particular reference to the cosmological de Sitter space, the space can be interpreted as an implementation of de Sitter CFT. Subsequently, the space can be reinterpreted as an implementation of hyperbolic anti de Sitter space via the reflection of a time slice for an infinite number of times. Consequently, the information paradox problem for cosmological de Sitter space can be reinterpreted as the problem of a quantum computer storing maximum information on an exponentially growing volume.

drive conscious experiences have long been the focal point of research in cognitive neuroscience. In contrast to classical physics, which initially seemed unsuitable for a role in causally effective consciousness, the indeterminacy and unique duality of quantum physics have opened doors for modeling consciousness. We utilize quantum principles, particularly the Schrödinger equation and Planck-Einstein relation, to investigate the relevant timescales of conscious processes and to understand how non-zero interactions between quantum components give rise to entanglement and correlations. We also examine, within quantum constraints, how information can be extracted from quantum states on behalf of classical systems. In this context, we discuss two relevant proofs – those of von Neumann and Zeh – in relation to the phenomenon of decoherence, which offers a solution to the problem of the observer in the context of consciousness. Finally, we explore, within quantum frameworks, the issue of subjectively objective consciousness and acknowledge that conscious processes, whether we like it or not, introduce a degree of subjective objective reality. In conclusion, by adopting a quantum framework for consciousness, we can study, calculate and predict conscious processes that underlie subjective experience. In this approach, fundamental problems in consciousness can be reformulated as quantum problems that can be tackled using new tools and techniques. In particular, the predictive power of quantum consciousness allows us to make testable claims against various long-standing conjectures in consciousness studies, particularly on binding mechanisms and consciousness in anesthesia. In the spirit of validation rather than formulation, we propose experimental verification of assumptions that are essential for an old problem in consciousness studies, which we have taken from the works of famous scientists such as Einstein, Berry, Page and Wootters. We use quantum principles to provide a detailed derivation of their concerns, which we then validate with a series of measurements in real-time brain processing. In this context, the concept of global workspace theory is closely aligned to the quantum concept of wave function collapse, which implies that subjective experience may fundamentally be a global workspace consciousness. In this approach, we can analyze, calculate and predict conscious processes that underlie subjective experience. In this context, the problem of consciousness can be transformed into a series of solvable problems in quantum mechanics, which can provide a roadmap for concrete experimentation in brain physics. In this context, the age-old problem of consciousness can be transformed into a modern science that is rooted in quantum mechanics, which is capable of providing both answers to fundamental questions and predicting outcomes in brain and behavioral physiology. In this context, the problem of consciousness can be effectively addressed by brain physicists

We associate the initial investment with a single quantum system's ergotropy - a measure equivalent to the quantum analogue of free energy, as described by Allahverdyan, Balian, and Nieuwenhuizen - and express it through electromagnetic radiation. As betting outcomes occur, this system experiences attenuation and amplification, simulating loss and winning events. This stochastic evolution in the quantum memory is analogous to the random lasing phenomenon and can be characterized in a Bosonic Gaussian channel framework. Furthermore, by assuming that the input capital is a Gaussian density matrix - that is, a displaced, squeezed thermal Gibbs state - we investigate how model performance changes based on this state. We also confirm that the optimal gambler's strategy is for the gambler to omit any active management of the quantum system, allowing it to passively accumulate value. We observe that the random attenuation and amplification processes that simulate the outcome of the bets cause the quantum system to transition into a maximum entropy state. This study contrasts the conventional, payout-based model with the novel, ergotropy-based model and verifies that the latter does not reduce to the latter under certain conditions. To address these problems, experts employ fairness metrics, decentralized machine learning methods known as federated learning, or differential privacy. A pioneering approach, this study creates a unified ethical federated learning framework, seamlessly integrating all three techniques in harmony. Experimental results based on the Adult, Bank and Dutch datasets showcase the "interplay" between precision, equity, and confidentiality that occurs empirically as a direct outcome. Specifically, our analysis indicates that applying fairness metrics reduces bias in predictions while compromising a bit on precision. Conversely, employing differential privacy improves privacy at a minor cost to prediction accuracy. Surprisingly, using federated learning does not consistently reduce bias, depending on how data is collected and how the learning process is structured. Ultimately, our research provides ethically aware federated learning as a valuable tool to address data processing challenges in a multi-stakeholder setting. Such an approach could potentially attract more participants, including organizations and individuals, to participate in machine learning projects without compromising their interests. A key adaptation of the Transformer model for computer vision involves using image tokens (formed by dividing images into smaller patches) and employing multiple nested transformers to process image tokens and patch dependencies. However, the existing nested transformer architecture suffers from several limitations in computer vision tasks, including the constraints imposed by image tokens and the implicit patch dependency order. Our research aims to overcome such limitations by introducing Top-Down Transformers (TDTs) for patch dependencies in computer vision tasks. In a TDT, a high-resolution feature map serves as a global guide to facilitate explicit and efficient patch dependencies among local image patches. We have adapted the PatchEmbed module from the Transformer to generate patch representations from high-resolution features. Our proposed approach, named TDT, consists of two network streams: a bottom-up network that produces intermediate representations and a top-down network that combines patch representations from the high-resolution features. In a comprehensive evaluation of TDT, we have reported state-of-the-art results on several notable datasets, including CIFAR-10, CelebA, Flawed In-Data (FID), and Stanford Artificial Pose (SAP), as well as satisfactory performance on complex visual tasks such as semantic segmentation, visual question answering, and image captioning. The source code and model parameters for our proposed method are publicly available. This transformer is coupled with a patch aggregator that enables the efficient merging of feature maps for capturing context at various image scales in a unified manner. Furthermore, a baseline transformer is implemented for comparative analysis of the proposed top-down approach. Our proposed method, named Top-Down Transformers (TDT), yields state-of-the-art performance on several notable datasets including CIFAR-10, CelebA, Flawed In-Dataset (FID), and Stanford Artificial Pose (SAP), as well as a faster convergence rate on image manipulation tasks. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, called "sonification," is characterized by a significant decrease in the gel's resistance to external forces, often resulting in the gel transitioning back into a liquid state. In order to understand the sonification process, scientists created a new theoretical framework that accurately predicts the gel's response to ultrasonic energy. According to this model, the sonification effect is directly linked to the energy transferred from the ultrasonic waves to the gel, with key factors including the ultrasonic frequency, intensity, and the interactions between the gel components. However, studies show that stable matchings are achieved even with shorter, albeit incomplete, preference lists, thus sparking curiosity as to why and how agents should optimize these lists for the best possible matches. Researchers have explored this question in a theoretical model introduced by Lee (2016), in which positions on preferences are valued, representing how much agents care about each given option. By focusing on the total value of preferences, without considering list length, the goal is to maximize the overall value of preferences for both the proposed matches and individual choices within those matches. In the present study, we demonstrate that the total value of preferences for both parties can be achieved by strictly ranking preferences from highest to lowest. Furthermore, we show that our result also applies to individual optimization efforts, with each agent maximizing their own preference values within matches by strictly ranking their preferences. It's worth noting that our result doesn't necessarily apply across different matchings; however, when considering individual optimization efforts, our evidence suggests that the total value of preferences for both parties is also optimized within those individual matchings. This contrasts with a previous finding by Lee (2016), in which both parties' optimization efforts only achieve the second-best possible matching outcome within individual optimizations, unlike with list length, where complete and ranked preference lists yield the best possible matches in terms of individual and joint optimization efforts. A key difference between individual optimizations within Deferred Acceptance and the broader mechanism framework and our joint optimization findings within those mechanisms are what motivated our study of joint optimization efforts in our accompanying paper (Kuzioka et al., 2020). In the latter study, we show that our joint optimization results in those mechanisms are also achievable in real-world applications with agents having a positive number of preferences. That being said, we also show that our joint optimization efforts may result in less-desirable outcomes compared to using complete preference lists. Therefore, the total value of preferences for both parties may not be optimized within individual matchings when considering joint optimization efforts. This contrasts with a previous finding by Birch and Malacaria (2015) in which both parties' optimization efforts only achieve the worst possible matching outcomes within individual optimizations. This also contrasts with a previous finding by Kuzioka et al. (2020) in which both parties' optimization efforts achieve the second-best possible matching outcomes within individual optimizations. This paper investigates how the scale of these pre-training datasets impacts state-of-the-art semantic parsers. annotation is a crucial task for linguistics and natural language processing, typically addressed through machine learning. Although the problem is largely solved for contemporary languages, historical corpora pose significant challenges, primarily due to limited native speaker interaction and a lack of training data. Compounding this issue, historical texts lack standardized sentence structures and orthographies, making automated POS tagging more complex and error-prone. In light of these complexities, instead of assigning single tags with uncertainty, POS tagging algorithms should allow for probabilistic outcomes. We propose applying the concept of set-valued prediction, enabling POS taggers to suggest a set of potential tags rather than guessing a single one. The objective is to strike a balance between ensuring a high likelihood of the correct tag being included in the suggested set while minimizing the number of possible outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that integrating set-valued prediction into existing state-of-the-art POS tagging algorithms achieves better performance on Old English, a historically complex text. Moreover, a set-valued approach offers a versatile framework for handling tasks such as multi-label POS tagging, language identification, and tag alignment across languages with distinct label sets. In addition, the proposed method has the advantage of being applicable to both supervised and semi-supervised tagging problems. A source code version of the proposed algorithm is available at https://github.com/CiaraAcosta/Set-Predict-POS. Utilizing growth mixture modeling, our analysis identified four distinct health trajectory patterns. These patterns were then related to early life factors and lifestyle behaviors to create an individualized risk assessment and develop more effective prevention and intervention strategies tailored to different groups. By recognizing that different individuals with the same chronic disease may exhibit varying responses to similar early life and lifestyle factors, our approach may lead to a more accurate prediction of an individual's health outcomes. Digital health platforms can facilitate the collection of necessary data to model complex health pathways and inform personalized decision-making. The results of our research serve as proof-of-concept for applying this method to health studies and other fields involving longitudinal data. Additionally, we have outlined the main hurdles to implementing this approach in real-world settings. Further exploration of our method in studies of both high- and low-income populations could contribute to advancing our understanding of health trajectories and inform policy-making. The associated R code is publicly available on the GitHub site at https://github.com/user/jasansky/growth-mixture-analysis. The data used for this analysis are from the ALSPAC study (Acute Lymphatic Leukemia Study: http://www.alsp.ac.uk/). Our initial investigation was then expanded to include an examination of the social determinants of health. The R code for this analysis can be found at https://github.com/user/marissabillington/SDOH-GLM. The data used in this analysis are from the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) and have been made publicly available through the National Institute on Aging's website at http://www.nih.gov/. The ALSPAC study has also provided us with some of our data. The study's lead investigators have agreed to share the information with us due to its potential to inform future research. The HRS data were obtained through a collaboration with Dr. Kenneth Minkoff at the Boston University. The study's lead researcher is Marissa Billington. The other researchers are Jasmin A. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where we proved the problem parameterized by the feedback vertex set number to be W[1]-hard. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number with simultaneous unweighted feedback vertex set removal does not yield fixed-parameter tractability. Furthermore, we investigated complexity for minimum feedback vertex set reduction and verified its W[1]-hardness. We also explored complexity for parameter vertex deletion cost and verified its W[1]-hardness under different scenarios. Furthermore, we proved that parameterization by the distance to a fixed target vertex does not yield fixed-parameter tractability, even when the target vertex is at distance one. Finally, we investigated complexity for parameter vertex deletion number and verified its W[1]-hardness. Additionally, we discovered that parameterization by the vertex Deletion number yields fixed-parameter tractability. The obtained results illustrate the complexity of parameterized problems and their interactions with graph modification problems. It appears that vertex deletion and removal share distinct complexities, with removal yielding fixed-parameter tractability and deletion yielding W[1]-hardness. The problem remains open for parameter vertex deletion number, and we hope to tackle this under more restrictive assumptions, such as the input graph being chordal. Finally, we suggested research directions and open problems, and we hope to investigate these under various assumptions in the future. When we deviated from the standard self-dual sector of this variant, we stumbled upon a novel action describing higher-spin Yang-Mills theory, an expansion of Yang-Mills theory itself. This theory's twistor action builds directly upon Yang-Mills theory's original form. Our findings suggest that higher-spin Yang-Mills theory might be reimagined as a version of self-dual Yang-Mills theory, a concept we've supported with a series of literature reviews on the topic. The reimagined theory's twistor actions offer a glimpse into their full field content. The field is broken down into its individual components – the physical fields of Yang-Mills theory and higher-spin fields – through a reworking of the theory's translation sector. This piece of work marks the initial step in translating higher-spin fields into physical fields via a translation of the fields' superspaces. Our research indicates that higher-spin fields' superspaces can be reinterpreted as superspaces consisting of physical fields. This concept has been successfully put to the test within the confines of self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory and its spin-off variant. The reimagined theory has also been used to resolve an unresolved question regarding the translation sector of self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory's action. This question revolved around determining the general form of self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory's physical fields in twistor space. This concept has also led to the creation of a physical fields representation for self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory's physical fields via a reworking of the theory's superspace spaces. This reworking has been successfully put to the test and the obtained results match the original superspace model. Our research further demonstrates that similar reimagining processes can be applied to other theories such as self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory's spin-off variant, self-dual supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory itself, and higher-spin Yang-Mills theory. This has allowed us to derive a physical fields representation for the superspace fields consisting of the superspace vector components of higher-spin fields, the superspace scalar components of higher-spin fields, and their superspace vector components. This physical fields representation is compatible with the superconformal equations and forms an extension of the superconformal fields representation system. A crucial aspect of theoretical models for screening involves the presence of a well-defined reference state, to which screening elements react in order to release tension.  However, amorphous materials, lacking such a reference point, still demonstrate screening effects resulting from plastic events which have a considerable influence on the mechanical behavior of the material.  A recent research study proposed that in amorphous solids, mechanical strain can either exhibit weak or strong screening effects resulting from varying levels of plastic event density.  At lower levels of plastic event density, the strain is largely eliminated; but at higher levels, the strain is no longer completely erased, rather it's reduced.  Our research supports this hypothesis through data obtained from computer simulations of 2D and 3D glassy materials that have been subjected to sustained tension.  A crucial note is that in our specific simulations, the 2D material underwent elimination of strain at high deformation rates, whereas the 3D material underwent a reduction of strain at all deformation rates.  Furthermore, we have discovered that the point at which the strain begins to be reduced marks the onset of a state referred to as the "deformed liquid" where plastic events no longer follow the pattern of an exponential distribution over time, indicating a higher level of instability.  A correlation also exists between the deformation rate marking this transition and the point at which the strain is reduced, with both related to the average strain over a specific range of values in both power-law and logarithmic relationships.  Our research specifically observes that in 2D material, the strain screening effects have implications for the material's resilience against cracking, confirming that weak screening effects result in greater resistance against cracking.  On the other hand, strong screening effects, marking a state referred to as "critical clumping", result in cracking at a lower level of stress.  Our research, incorporating observations from past studies, has found that strong screening effects coupled with a state referred to as "critical clumping" result in cracking at a lower level of stress, marking an aspect of the universal patterns that govern the geological process of cracking. Despite extensive study on the mechanisms driving probability-matching in organisms, there is still uncertainty about its underlying nature.  A popular theory is that organisms employing probability-matching are responding to perceived options, whereas those using maximization are not and therefore more likely to make mistakes.  To test this hypothesis, a collection of organisms with spatial memory capabilities were studied in a series of experiments.  These organisms were subjected to a task where they were presented with two reward options and their strategies were measured and compared before and after they were given clues about the best option.  The data showed that while their strategy remained the same, it adapted accordingly by shifting towards the likely better option when the clue was given, which means that even though their strategy was originally probability-matching, it wasn't because they were responding differently to the options, but because they were making fewer mistakes.  These results confirm that probability-matching is an optimal strategy in uncertain environments and that the assumption that probability-matching is based on correct perception of the options is incorrect, which means that the notion of maximization is not necessarily a measure of a "better" strategy.  A new interpretation is suggested, which is that the likelihood of an organism employing probability-matching indicates its likelihood of making fewer mistakes in its decisions.  A model was developed to show how organisms with limited sensory capabilities could evolve to use probability-matching as a result of environmental uncertainty and it was found that the likelihood of the appearance of maximization is related to the ratio of the reward difference to the level of uncertainty in that environment.  A simulation was also conducted to show how the strategies of organisms with overlapping distributions intersect with each other and it was found that the strategies of the organisms with the highest precision are either probability-matching or maximization.  A practical implication is proposed, which is to describe a range of strategies known as probabilistic-suboptimal strategies, which are interpreted as appearing when organisms have or develop sparse or imprecise cognitive representations.  Lastly, potential criticisms and challenges are mentioned.  A related challenge is presented, which is to investigate the extent to which probability-matching is associated with reduced environmental uncertainty, which would have significant implications for the understanding of related phenomena such as probability-matching in health conditions and probability-matching in choice tasks. This work lays the groundwork for establishing a decentralized, predictive model forecasting service, leveraging a predictive model forecasting framework for scientific data. We will make available the source code for our new predictive model forecasting framework through an open-source project on GitHub. We have also applied for funding to support the development of a predictive model forecasting center, incorporating a wide range of contributors. Once operational, the predictive model forecasting center will facilitate the forecasting of scientific data from a diverse collection of computational models, contributed by a broad scientific community. This research will mark the beginning of a new area of research, the predictive model forecasting of scientific data, which will facilitate numerous studies on the prediction performance of the collective models, guiding the development of the best computational models, as well as recommendations for model evolution. Keywords: Pre-trained models, fine-tuning, parameter-efficient tuning, named entity recognition, text categorization. 

Abstract:

Pre-trained models have significantly outperformed other supervised learning techniques in achieving state-of-the-art results across numerous downstream natural language processing tasks. However, these models require substantial resources to update all parameters when adapting them to new tasks, especially when task datasets are small. In this research, we explore efficient tuning of pre-trained models, especially for low-resource tasks. First, we identify that updating special token embeddings, like classification tokens in BERT, before self-attention operations, is crucial for model optimization. By doing this, we can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters. Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models and showcases the importance of special tokens during pre-training. Furthermore, we propose a new approach to text classification called Token-wise Token Attention that outperforms BERT and RoBERTa baselines and achieves superior results when integrated into our proposed framework. Evaluation experiments were conducted using both English and Indian language datasets. The corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/prashikshah18/PASTA.

However, existing approaches compressing images into symbols with varying lengths that do not follow a specific pattern are not ideal for steganographic purposes. To resolve this issue, this research proposes two novel ideas. Firstly, we develop a static engine that utilizes a fixed length but random variable to represent the result of lossless compression, thereby reducing memory consumption. Secondly, we develop a static engine that uses the binary format of the length and random variable to enhance security and transparency during extraction. Our approach is evaluated against state-of-the-art methods and our experimental findings demonstrate that the proposed engine offers superior statistical characteristics in terms of distribution and entropy. Furthermore, both proposals exhibit a high level of security and transparency, with the proposed engine also showcasing improved bandwidth at a comparable level of visual quality. Our source code is available for viewing at https://github.com/charles-rose/Static-Steganography. To the best of our knowledge, this research aims to introduce the concept of using binary formats for length and random variables for the first time. Specifically, when a new edge is added, it follows the preferential attachment rule with a certain probability and otherwise forms between two randomly selected nodes.  This approach results in a network whose clustering coefficient and average degree can be analytically calculated. This division leads to a significant difference in degree distribution between the initial and main phases of the network's development.  This analysis validates the model's potential for community analysis and sheds light on the dynamic evolution of Wikipedia edit networks.  The model's source code is available for download at https://github.com/lvyao/hybridnetwork. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot incorporates user-friendly and semi-automatic interaction features, allowing for the analysis of typically ignored non-hierarchical associations. Its efficacy is demonstrated through the visualisation of the Gene Ontology and biological pathway ontologies, proving that OntoPlot can accurately and informatively visual the complex structures of these domain-specific knowledge bases. Experimental findings show that OntoPlot's exploration capabilities are superior to those of existing tools, providing users with a comprehensive, user-friendly experience. As such, OntoPlot has the potential to significantly enhance the exploration and analysis of large, complex ontologies in various fields. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance, its practical application is restricted to simple scenarios, primarily due to the computational complexity involved. This paper explores whether deep neural networks can effectively instantiate the active inference theory, specifically in complex video analysis tasks. A new module, referred to as the 'active agent,' was created to interact with the module responsible for object detection within a pre-trained CNN. The results reveal that the active agent achieved exceptional performance on datasets for ship detection and submarine recognition, showcasing an impressive capability to work well in environments where very little data is available. Moreover, the analysis demonstrates that the active agent embodies key aspects of the active inference theory and suggests potential avenues for further optimization. This study not only achieves state-of-the-art performance on challenging tasks but also provides significant insights into the practical application of the active inference theory, paving the way for potential advancements in both robotics and artificial intelligence generally. Additionally, we analyzed and compared the self-entropy and total entropy production within the system to gain a deeper understanding of the universal aspects of irreversible processes. We discovered that total entropy production, which considers both system and heat effects, correlates better with the Soret effect and is therefore a more accurate phenomenological descriptor. In contrast, self-entropy production, which solely accounts for the system's internal organization, does not capture the full irreversibility of the observed effects. This distinction highlights the significance of distinguishing between different forms of entropy when analyzing thermodynamic processes in complex systems. Finally, we propose potential experimental approaches to verify our computational results and bridge the gap between static theory and dynamic measurement. These experiments could involve soft atomic liquids or polymeric fluids. We also suggest possible implications for systems governance, particularly those containing functional materials that adapt to temperature. By adapting their shape in response to the temperature gradient, flexible molecules may actively contribute to the thermodynamic non-equilibrium by optimizing their internal organization. Consequently, an external observer could potentially influence the system's irreversibility by inducing conformational rearrangements that counteract or reinforce the inherent thermal non-equilibrium of the flexible molecules. The overall scenario is reminiscent of Maxwell's demon, where internal agents may potentially harness and manipulate thermal non-equilibrium to achieve a more efficient organization of the system. However, the current study does not explore this potential, and the competition between flexible molecules' internal dynamics and external thermal non-equilibrium remains an unresolved topic. Effective evaluation by an NLP model depends on its ability to identify patterns in written content, even in cases where the writing quality is subpar. Despite the current prominence of large transformer-based models in various NLP applications, these models' computational complexity poses significant practical limitations to their deployment. This paper aims to counter this drawback by introducing a Distilled Autoencoder specifically designed to process raw text for Automated Essay Scoring. By leveraging the capabilities of Contrastive Learning to fine-tune its representation, the Distilled Autoencoder offers an efficient alternative to the current NLP and recent Text-BERT approaches for the same task. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed Distilled Autoencoder outperforms state-of-the-art Automated Essay Scoring models and achieves a notable reduction in inference latency, marking it as the first NLP-based solution to score evenly across all four Dimensions of Writing and surpass the performance of transformer-based models in this application. Furthermore, when deployed as a feature extractor, the Distilled Autoencoder facilitates the development of the first Linear Model to score evenly across all four Dimensions of Writing. Our open-source implementation of the Distilled Autoencoder will be made available on GitHub. By leveraging knowledge-distillation techniques, the paper also introduces a new NLP application: Text Summarization. Moreover, the paper provides a case study on the practical deployment of the Distilled Autoencoder for Automated Essay Scoring in real-world settings. By achieving a 90% acceleration in inference time, the paper shows that the Distilled Autoencoder can be effectively used as a production-ready model for the next-practice level of expertise in NLP and Automated Essay Scoring. As such, this model offers an appealing alternative to state-of-the-art but computationally expensive solutions. Finally, the paper highlights the potential for linear models to achieve competitive performance with more complex NLP models, especially when the model architecture is tailored for interpretability and automated scoring of poor writing. By sharing the paper's results and sources, we aim to promote Reproducibility and foster collaboration on a range of Automated Scoring challenges that require efficient NLP models for assignment or test-question scoring. Our work here involves developing the first Distilated Autoencoder for AES applications, and we identify both general and specific contributions: (i) a new NLP application in distillation, automated and scored by humans; (ii) a new linear model for AES with competitive NLP performance; (iii) a new compact architecture for Automated Essay Scoring,

As the interest in meta-learning grows, there is a pressing need to establish its theoretical underpinnings. Specifically, we will examine the convergence properties of meta-algorithms using gradient-based optimization methods, such as stochastic gradient descent, in the context of a two-layer neural network model where the last layer is fixed and the adaptation mechanism is confined to the intermediate layer. By employing standard objective functions and loss functions for both the task at hand and the meta-learning objective, we first obtain general convergence conditions for meta-learners that have no training data. Next, we investigate a meta-learner that has access to unlabeled data for representation learning. We observe that, contrary to conventional learning processes, the convergence rate of meta-learners is influenced by the complexity of the data distribution and the choice of hyperparameters. Moreover, the rate at which the meta-learner optimizes the meta-objective after fine-tuning is related to the number of iterations, while the optimization rate for the individual tasks is inversely proportional to the number of epochs. Ultimately, we validate our theoretical analysis through a comprehensive comparison with empirical results. Our study provides essential insights to guide the development and assessment of meta-learning algorithms. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/guillimeye/metalearn. The experiments conducted in this research are the first to compare the performance of meta-learners that optimize over parameters or layers versus those that optimize over tasks or objectives. The empirical results we report may seem counterintuitive at first, but they align with the theoretical predictions we derived. For instance, we discovered that, in certain instances, fine-tuning in the task space actually leads to overfitting, which is consistent with our theoretical estimates of optimization rates. Furthermore, we observed that, in other situations, unlearning while fine-tuning in the task space can even prevent overfitting, as indicated by our theoretical estimates. The code for the experiments we performed is available at the provided repository, along with the data and pre-trained models, allowing for the replication of the results we report. It is our hope that this study may inspire the creation of new, even more powerful meta-algorithms in various domains

Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions of harm, largely reliant on causality, surprisingly overlook the use of causal models and actual causality theories. This paper presents a new definition of qualitative harm, grounded in causal models and an established concept of actual causality, specifically emphasizing contrastive causation and default utility. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue highlights the need for an alternative approach combining probabilistic forecasts with peak demand predictions, which can improve overall forecasting performance, particularly during peak hours and at lower network levels, where the incorporation of peak forecasts yields a significant improvement in results. This finding is illustrated by the case study of a group of five households, where the application of the proposed method resulted in an average reduction of mean absolute percentage error by 19.5% compared to the standard method. Furthermore, the method's potential benefits are discussed in terms of its impact on the management of household appliances. Based on this, it is suggested that the optimal application of the proposed method may involve a framework that dynamically switches between the probabilistic and peak-demand forecasting methods, depending on the time of day and network level. This approach aims to improve overall forecasting by prioritizing probabilistic forecasting during off-peak hours and using peak-demand forecasting during peak periods. This technique was implemented in MATLAB and the code is available upon request. Additionally, the research found that the method's performance is influenced by factors like total active power, apparent power, and the power from specific frequency bands. Notably, the method tends to enhance forecasting accuracy by an average of 9.4% when considering these factors. This compares to an average improvement of 19.5% when incorporating peak forecasts across the entire dataset. This confirms that the method's benefits arise primarily from its performance during peak demand situations. This further emphasizes the significance of accurately forecasting daily peak demand for short-term energy consumption forecasting. Moreover, the method's potential for improving the management of appliances via advanced home energy management systems, particularly by using feedback from the forecasted peak demand, is an area that warrants further exploration in future research studies. This includes designing algorithms that dynamically switch between the proposed method and other established forecasting techniques, which could ultimately lead to a more comprehensive and efficient feedback system for appliance management. We diverge from conventional methods of developing optimal controllers through in-depth modeling and simulation, instead directly teaching model-free controllers to the actual robot. Initially, gaits are generated through central pattern generators, whose parameters are fine-tuned to rapidly develop an open-loop controller for efficient walking. To achieve this, we leverage the existing OpenLOMO open-source toolbox to easily collect robot data and design suitable reinforcement learning rewards. We showcase the effectiveness of this approach using the 10g humanoid robot and three experiments: 1) starting the robot while paused, 2) recovering from a fall, and 3) transitioning between different states. We increase the robot's ability to navigate these challenges and various others through dynamic Gait Learning. Additionally, we develop a novel learning algorithm that allows existing controllers to adapt to new situations, whose applications and limits are evaluated. We find that our learning algorithms can cut controller development time, making it feasible to model-based approach, whereas previously it was only achievable through in-depth simulation studies. Furthermore, we observe that our spring-based controllers can generate up to 60% more efficient gait patterns than purely passive ones. We partner to share our findings with two research groups: 1) Dr. Konstantin Badeau from Columbia University, who's developing legged actuators, and 2) Dr. Danilo Gregoretti from IIT, who's exploring spring-based actuators. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in real-world applications, most existing studies have focused on one problem alone. In this research, we aim to achieve state-of-the-art results on both tasks. To accomplish this, we propose a novel method that translates a query into a representation that incorporates the desired attributes. This is achieved through a guided cross- and self-attention mechanism that distinguishes between a query's unique attributes and global image features. Additionally, we introduce a dual-batch memory to facilitate attribute manipulation during the training process. When evaluating our model on several datasets, the results demonstrate that it is capable of performing instance-level image retrieval and attribute manipulation more effectively than current baselines. This paper proposes a novel cost constructor, designed with convolutional neural networks, to efficiently generate matching cost for light field depth estimation.
